---
title: "Teaching with studysim"
---

```{r}
source("_common.R")
```

Each exercise below names the scenario and options, then what the students should
find. The tables are the answer key's *expected estimates* (one large simulated
study), computed by the module itself when this page was built.

## Confounding: coffee and coronary heart disease

*Coronary heart disease incidence*, cohort, measure age, sex, smoking and coffee.
Coffee has no effect, but coffee drinkers smoke more: the crude hazard ratio of
coffee is above 1 and disappears once smoking is in the model.

```{r}
key_table("chd_incidence", "chd", "cohort", c("age", "sex", "smoking", "coffee"))
```

Exercise: leave smoking unmeasured and show that the adjusted coffee effect stays
biased (residual confounding).

## Confounding by indication: chemotherapy

*Breast cancer prognosis*, prognosis design. Chemotherapy truly lowers the hazard
(HR 0.75), but it is given to younger women with more nodes and higher grade; its
crude hazard ratio points the wrong way.

```{r}
key_table("breast_cancer_prognosis", "death", "prognosis", c("age", "tumour_size", "nodes", "grade", "chemo"))
```

## Odds ratios from a case-control study

*Breast cancer risk factors*, case-control with two controls per case. The data are
generated as a cohort with hazard ratios; the case-control odds ratios approach them
because the disease is rare. Menopause has no effect of its own, but is determined
by age (a rule of the scenario): its crude odds ratio is pure confounding.

```{r}
key_table("breast_cancer_risk", "breast_cancer", "case_control", c("age", "menopause", "parity", "family_hist", "alcohol"),
          options = list(ratio = 2))
```

Exercise: compare with *Matched case-control* on age, analysed with conditional
logistic regression.

## Effect modification

In the same scenario BMI protects before menopause and raises risk after it. A
model without the interaction gives a single, misleading BMI effect; students
should fit `bmi × menopause`. The answer key shows the true effect per level of
menopause in its note.

## Categorising a continuous variable

Systolic pressure in quartiles (*Form: quartiles*) gives a dose-response pattern
but loses information: compare the precision of the per-10-mmHg estimate with the
quartile contrasts, and the effect of choosing other cut points.

```{r}
key_table("chd_incidence", "chd", "cohort", c("age", "sex", "sbp"), categorize = list(sbp = list(form = "quartiles")))
```

## Trials: parallel and crossover

*Antihypertensive drug vs placebo*: in the parallel trial the unadjusted difference
is unbiased, and adjusting for baseline pressure (ANCOVA) narrows the interval. In
the 2×2 crossover each patient is their own control: 30 patients give a precise
estimate, and the period effect must be in the model.

```{r}
key_table("antihypertensive_trial", "sbp", "rct", c("sbp0", "age"))
key_table("antihypertensive_trial", "sbp", "crossover", character())
```

*Bioequivalence*: AUC and Cmax are log-normal; analyse log values and back-transform
to a geometric mean ratio, then check whether its 90% CI lies within 0.80–1.25.

## Assignments with student keys

Give every student the same options and their own **student key** (e.g. their ID):
each gets a different dataset from the same superpopulation. The teacher reproduces
any of them by typing the key, and the answer key is the same for all.
